newsitem.title: UK: Gold market "understandably" worried over EMU - GFMS.
newsitem.headline: Gold market "understandably" worried over EMU - GFMS.

text.p: The gold market is "understandably" concerned about how tightly held Europe Union (EU) countries' gold reserves will be with the coming of European Monetary Union (EMU), according to a report released on Wednesday.

"The prospect of European Monetary Union has for the first time in a generation put gold back on the agenda for Europe's central banks," market analysts Gold Fields Mineral Services Ltd said in its Gold 1997 report.

The report, compiled before news that the world's potentially largest gold find at Busang in Indonesia was a sham, also noted the EU countries hold 39 per cent of the world's gold reserves. With Switzerland, the western European central banks account for 46 percent of the world total or twice as much as the United States.
As well as EMU, the banks like others worldwide are endeavouring to more actively manage their reserves.
"A new generation of managers without the reverence for gold of their predecessors is inclined to view their bullion reserves as little different in principle from foreign exchange," the report said.
The European banks' gold reserves are also largely measured against their foreign exchange reserves averaging 31 percent of reserves versus a world average of 13 percent.
The Maastricht Treaty on EMU only gives policy guidelines against which to measure the impact of EMU on gold and foreign exchange reserves.
But it does envisage the transfer of around $60 billion to the European Central bank in non EU-foreign exchange and gold.
The treaty also notes that that whereas the central banks may buy and sell gold, such operations above an unspecified limit will require the approval of the ECB.
"The gold market thus fears that there could be pre-emptive gold sales while countries still have autonomy in the run up to EMU," according to the report.

The pressure to act quickly is increased as after the ECB is established, the banks will be even more overweight in gold as holdings in the currencies of other members states...will disappear following EMU."
Some banks like the Swedish national bank and the Bundesbank have not indicated that they intend to revalue their gold at market prices from current low book values.
But Switzerland, the only major nation with a gold-backed currency, does intend to revalue its reserves at above the current $96 per ounce book value.

Furthermore, it intends to abolish the rule requiring 40 percent of gold backing for its note issue and to sell some of this gold to raise funds for a humanitarian institution, the Swiss Foundation for Solidarity -- financed from the gains achieved from revaluing gold.
"The Swiss development may also increase the chance of eventual IMF (International Monetary Fund) gold sales..." the report said.
"As a result it is possible that the shelved proposal to sell five percent (161 tonnes) of the Fund's gold could be renewed in the near future," the report added.
